analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the federal housing department and replaces its aid programs with time-limited vouchers and state block grants.
analysis.headline: A bill with 59 cosponsors to abolish HUD never got a committee vote and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have shut down the Department of Housing and Urban Development, winding it up by 2000. It would have ended public housing, project-based rental aid, AIDS housing, and homeless assistance programs, replacing them with block grants to states and a federal voucher program that helps low-income families rent or buy homes — but only for up to five years per family. It would also have ended new FHA mortgage insurance and shifted that business to private mortgage insurers operating with a federal fund behind them.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income families who receive the new vouchers could use them to rent or, if first-time buyers, to purchase a home, with the freedom to choose any qualifying unit [S3]. Taxpayers would benefit from the bill's stated goal of reducing federal housing spending by consolidating and eliminating programs [S3]. States and public housing agencies would gain wide flexibility, since most programs would be folded into block grants they could spend on locally chosen housing activities [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, states, and some low-income renters

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal housing voucher program giving low-income families monthly help with rent or first-time homeownership costs, letting each family choose its own dwelling and move within a state or metro area [S3].

Folds many housing programs into block grants with a requirement that at least 90 percent of funds serve low-income people, plus set-asides for elderly, disabled, AIDS-affected, and Indian housing [S2].
Reduces federal spending for housing and community development by consolidating and eliminating programs, the bill's stated purpose [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Long-term poor renters would lose the guarantee of continued help: vouchers would end after 60 months for anyone who is not elderly or disabled [S3]. Public housing residents, tenants in project-based section 8 buildings, people with AIDS, and homeless people in shelter-plus-care would see their dedicated programs terminated and replaced with state-run block grants [S2]. Taxpayers would backstop a new federal fund that pays losses to private mortgage insurers taking over FHA's single-family insurance business [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Long-term poor renters and public housing residents

drawbacks.text: Voucher help would be cut off after five years per family, except for elderly and disabled families — ending the promise of long-term rental assistance for working poor families who remain poor [S3].
Terminates public housing, project-based section 8, AIDS housing (HOPWA), shelter-plus-care homeless assistance, and other programs, leaving states to decide what to fund under block grants [S2].

Ends new FHA mortgage insurance and instead lets 'qualified mortgage insurers' share risk with a federal fund that pays their losses — moving a public insurance program into private hands with taxpayers absorbing covered losses [S2].

Transfers fair housing enforcement to the Justice Department while explicitly carving out the Fair Housing Initiatives Program from the transfer, leaving that enforcement-support program with no home [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill preserved a real benefit — portable vouchers for low-income families — and imposed a 90 percent low-income floor on block grant spending. But its central trade was to make housing aid temporary rather than a stable guarantee: five years of voucher help, then out. Families who stay poor through no brief emergency — disabled family members excluded, the working poor in high-rent cities — would lose the floor beneath them. Meanwhile the mortgage insurance title hands FHA's market to private insurers with a federal fund paying their losses, which shifts profit to private firms while keeping risk with taxpayers. The savings and the flexibility are real; so is the loss of long-term security for the poorest renters.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to two committees and then to subcommittees on housing and on government management, but neither panel ever acted, and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997 [S5].

narrative.text: Sam Brownback introduced the bill on August 4, 1995, with 59 cosponsors — 58 Republicans and 1 Democrat — including House Majority Leader Dick Armey and Majority Whip Tom DeLay [S3].
It was referred to the Banking and Financial Services Committee and the Government Reform and Oversight Committee on the day of introduction [S5].

In late August and early September 1995 it was sent to the Subcommittee on Government Management, Information and Technology and the Subcommittee on Housing and Community Opportunity; no markup or floor vote ever followed [S5].
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill expired without any vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public housing residents, section 8 tenants, and other low-income renters kept the housing programs the bill would have terminated, and HUD survived. No one else gained materially; the bill simply never moved.

for.name: Rep. Sam Brownback
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to abolish HUD and restructure federal housing aid.

for.name: 58 of 230 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the House Majority Leader and Majority Whip.

against.name: House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never reported it out; no markup is recorded in the action history.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Housing and Community Opportunity
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 1, 1995 and took no further recorded action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 59 cosponsors were Republicans except one Democrat, and no Democrat-sponsored opposition or floor vote is recorded; the bill stalled entirely in committee.

industries.note: The bill would ban new FHA insurance and let private 'qualified mortgage insurers' take over single-family mortgage insurance under risk-sharing deals, with a federal fund created to pay their covered losses [S2][S3]. They would gain a large government-built market while taxpayers stand behind the losses.

industries.industry: Mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac
industries.note: Ginnie Mae, the public mortgage guarantor, would be terminated, and the bill allows Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, or other private secondary-market firms to absorb its functions [S3]. Their federal regulator (OFHEO) would move to Treasury, retaining oversight of their safety and soundness [S3].

industries.industry: State governments and public housing agencies
industries.note: They would gain broad flexibility as most programs convert to block grants with deregulated public housing authorities and waiver authority [S2]. But they would also absorb responsibility for populations now served by dedicated federal programs, with federal funding consolidated and reduced [S2].
